course.title: Machine Design
course.instructor_note: The instructor is identifiable from the course's own handouts, and is the same instructor who wrote the ENGR 305 FEA report template. Rules the two packs share therefore come from one source, not two independent ones. No name is recorded.

coverage.notes: The executive-summary memo is the best-evidenced format in this pack: the instructor wrote a one-page model memo for a homework, with the answer left as placeholders, and one student memo follows it closely. Everything else is thinner. Module homework prompts are typed and readable, but most answers are handwritten on the printed prompt, so how a worked solution should look is not covered. One time-stepping set has typed answers inline. There is no syllabus, no rubric beyond the one project handout, and no graded returns. Methods come from the prompts themselves, from the model memo, and from the student's test-correction notes. The SolidWorks study in the OneDrive archive is a native results database with no readable text. It was opened on a second pass and shows only a single-part linear static study with no contacts, so it says nothing about what a deliverable must show. Coverage gap: a student-built, module-numbered calculator workbook in the same archive (the student's own tool, not an instructor document) spans ten topics: eccentric bolts, screw jacks, welds and adhesives, fatigue, shafts, bearings, drive trains, hydraulics, springs, and brakes and clutches. The methods in this pack reach only two of those ten topics (bolts, including eccentric groups and preload torque, and welds). Hand-versus-FEA reconciliation and the time-stepping exercise are not among the ten. So most of the course's method content is not covered here. A textbook method for the rest is not a course convention, and none is recorded. Not used: the archive also holds a top-level file named for the 2025 ENGR 322 final exam and a solution key. Their file metadata says a script generated them and the student edited them, the key was created a minute after the exam, and the exam tells the reader to use the student's own calculator. The student was asked where they came from and answered that he or an AI tool generated them for practice. They are not instructor material, so the exclusion is permanent and the question is closed: nothing in this pack is derived from them, and no exam rule, checklist, exam profile or topic list should ever be taken from them.

course_policy.summary: No syllabus or generative-AI policy for this course was found in the archive.

format.deliverable: Module homework, often closed by a one-page executive-summary memo; short hands-on labs; one presentation project; test corrections.
format.not_a_technical_memo: In ENGR 322 the prose deliverable is called an executive summary and uses a memo header (To, From, CC, Date, Re) with a short body. It has no title page, no abstract and no appendices. It is a different document from the title-page-plus-abstract 'technical memo' of ENGR 319 and 328. The words collide twice: 'memo' names both documents, and ENGR 328 uses 'executive summary' for the abstract block on its title page. Producing the other course's document here would look correct and be wrong.
precedence: the specific module or project prompt

artifacts.submitted: screenshots only, in the memo or write-up
not stated; the time-stepping answers say the instructor probably will not open it

pipeline_support.note: The memo is a one-page text document in a format the renderer produces (docx/pdf). This pack states three format.rendering fields (no title page, no abstract, no page numbers); see rendering_basis. Drafted as document_type "memo" with a memo_header, it renders with its To/From/CC/Date/Re block; a memo draft missing that header is refused rather than rendered incomplete. It is unverified until inspected. The renderer cannot produce the hand calculations or the FEA model the memo summarises. The student must supply those results, and the memo must not state agreement between methods that were not both run.

rendering_basis.title_page: spec: the instructor's model executive-summary memo starts with its To/From/CC/Date/Re header at the top of page 1, with no title page; the student's memo and test corrections do the same
rendering_basis.abstract: spec: the instructor's model memo has no abstract. Its first body paragraph carries the answer, and that paragraph is not a separate abstract block
rendering_basis.number_body_pages: spec: the instructor's model memo is one page with no page number; the student's memo and test corrections carry none either
rendering_basis.memo_header: The executive-summary memo is a header memo. The renderer lays it out when the draft declares document_type "memo" with a memo_header giving to, date and re (cc optional; from defaults to the run identity): a To/From/CC/Date/Re block under a rule, then the body, and no title page. It refuses a memo draft without that header, so a headerless 322 executive summary can no longer render as if complete. To is the instructor, filled from the student's own assignment sheet. The three stated fields still govern only page furniture.
rendering_basis.one_block_two_families: This pack holds one rendering block. The executive-summary memo and the test corrections are the only families that render as documents, and they agree on the three stated fields. Fields where the evidence disagrees or is missing are omitted and fall to the renderer's defaults.

omitted.table_captions_above: No evidence: the model memo has no tables, and no rendered 322 deliverable in the archive does either.
omitted.figure_captions_below: No evidence: the model memo has no figures. The one looser student summary has screenshots under plain labels, not captions.
omitted.body_font_size: They disagree, and there is no written rule. The instructor's model memo is set in 9 pt Arial (measured); the student's memo uses 11 pt Arial, and the test corrections a 12 pt default.
omitted.margin_inches: Not one value. The instructor's model memo has 1.25 in side margins but its header starts about 0.75 in from the top (measured), and the renderer takes one margin for all sides. The student's documents use 1 in.
omitted.line_spacing: Not stated. The renderer reads line_spacing as a leading ratio in PDF and as a Word multiple in docx, so no one value reproduces the model in both.

header.layout: One field per line, label then a tab, at the top of the page. No title page.

paragraphs: What was solved and by which methods (by hand and by FEA), with the bottom-line answer and the safety-factor basis in the first paragraph.
How closely the methods agreed, as a percentage, and any FEA anomaly and how it was handled.
How the hand calculation was done, which approximation it made, and which direction that biases the answer.
One short paragraph per secondary question in the prompt.
A closing sentence of confidence that restates the answer.
body.voice: First person singular is used in the instructor's own model. Short declarative paragraphs, no headings, no figures.

executive_summary_memo.looser_variant: One other student executive summary, for an FEA study with no surviving prompt, used a single title line instead of the memo header, with screenshots under plain labels. Its format is not endorsed by any instructor document. Use the memo form unless the prompt says otherwise.

methods.title: Solve by hand and by FEA, then reconcile
methods.when: Any module homework whose prompt says to check the answer, and the FEA study.
methods.shared_with: engr305 (same instructor: one source, not independent agreement)
steps: Solve by hand first, and write down every simplifying assumption the hand method makes.
Build the FEA model with the same geometry, material and supports as the hand model, using a material the software library actually has.
Compare the same quantity at the same location. Report the difference as a percentage.
Where FEA shows a single-node spike at a sharp corner, weld root or load point, read the stress at the surrounding nodes instead, and say so.
Explain the difference: which approximation in which method, and whether it makes the hand answer higher or lower.
State the answer both methods support, and whether you trust it.
pitfalls: Treating a singular corner stress as the real maximum.
Claiming agreement without saying what was compared where.
Supports in the FEA that are stiffer or looser than the hand model assumes.

methods.title: Size a fillet weld by treating the weld group as a line
steps: Treat each weld as a line of unit throat. Compute the group's centroid, and its unit second moment (Iu) or unit polar moment (Ju).
Find the direct shear per unit length, and the bending or torsional shear per unit length at the most distant point of the weld.
Combine them as vectors at that point to get the resultant force per unit length.
Divide by the allowable shear for the electrode to get the throat, then convert the throat to a leg size.
Check that the plates themselves are not the weaker element.
pitfalls: Basing the allowable on the base metal. With a matched electrode on mild steel, the electrode governs, which is why switching between similar mild steels barely changes the size.
Approximating J as a sum over a few discrete pieces underestimates it, which overstates the stress. That is conservative, but say so.

methods.title: Safety factor for each bolt in an eccentrically loaded group
methods.when: Bolted brackets or plates carrying an off-centre load.
steps: Locate the bolt-group centroid and the load's moment arm about it.
Split the load into direct shear (shared equally) and moment shear (proportional to each bolt's distance from the centroid, divided by the sum of squared distances).
Add them as vectors at each bolt, and find the worst-loaded bolt.
Compare against the grade's strength using the correct area (shank or thread) for where the shear plane falls.
Report a safety factor for each bolt, and answer any substitution question (grade, size, thread pitch) by rerunning with the new values.
pitfalls: Using the shank area when the shear plane passes through the threads.
Mixing metric and inch sizes when a substitute bolt is specified.

methods.title: Tightening torque for a target preload
methods.when: Fastener homework and the torque-wrench lab.
steps: Pick the preload: a stated fraction of proof load, or your own justified value.
Choose the nut factor K for the surface condition (dry, plated, or lubricated, from the course's fastener guide). Dry is highest and lubricated lowest.
Compute torque as K times preload times nominal diameter, with consistent units.
Comment on whether the torque is large for a hand tool.
pitfalls: Using one K value for every finish.
Taking bolt strength from an unchecked online chart. The prompt warns about exactly this.

methods.title: Explicit time stepping in a spreadsheet
methods.when: The time-stepping computer problems: motion driven first by a given acceleration, later by forces.
steps: Solve the simplest case analytically with calculus first, so the spreadsheet has a check.

Build columns for time, acceleration, velocity and position. Each new velocity is the previous velocity plus the previous acceleration times the step, and each new position is the previous position plus the previous velocity times the step.
Use the step size the prompt gives, then vary it and report how the answer changes.
For a force-driven version, compute the force from the current speed (a motor torque curve through the drive ratio), then the acceleration from the net force, then step forward.
Plot acceleration, velocity and position against time.
pitfalls: Never testing the step size, even though the prompt asks how the step affects the answer.
Using the current rather than the previous value in an explicit update, so the scheme no longer matches the stated equations.

write a one-page memo summarising the result
what_good_looks_like: The first paragraph gives the answer, with units and its safety-factor basis, so a reader could stop there.
The agreement between methods is stated as a number, and any FEA artefact is named and handled.
The hand method's approximation is named, with the direction it pushes the answer.
Every secondary question in the prompt gets its own short paragraph.
It fits on one page, with no headings or figures.

magnitudes.quantity: percent difference between hand calculation and FEA for the same quantity at the same location
magnitudes.basis: Handout: the instructor's model executive-summary memo presents hand and FEA answers within 15% of each other as acceptable. That is an example, not a stated target, and the upper bound of 20 is a plausibility margin, not a course rule.
magnitudes.note: Well above 20: usually a single-node spike at a sharp corner, weld root or load point read as the maximum, different quantities or locations compared, or supports stiffer or looser than the hand model assumes.

magnitudes.quantity: bolt preload as a fraction of proof load
magnitudes.basis: Handout and physical plausibility: the fasteners homework says a preload of 75% of proof load is often used. The bounds around it are machine-design practice (up to about 0.9 for permanent joints), not a course rule.
magnitudes.note: Above 1: the bolt would yield when tightened, or the tensile-stress area and the proof strength were mismatched. Below 0.5 with no stated reason: check which strength was used.

magnitudes.basis: Handout and physical plausibility: the fasteners homework gives typical K values of roughly 0.14 lubricated, 0.2 zinc-plated and 0.25 dry. The bounds are a margin around those, from published torque coefficients.
magnitudes.note: Outside the range: not a nut factor, most often a friction coefficient or a percent. The same K for every finish in a comparison question is a method error even inside the range.

magnitudes.quantity: tightening torque for a hand-tool bolt (about 1/4 to 3/4 in)
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: T = K x F x d with a proof-load-scale preload gives single to low hundreds of lbf-ft across that size span.
magnitudes.note: About 12x high: lbf-in labelled lbf-ft. Near or below 1: the diameter went in as feet, or the preload in kips was read as lbf. A range cannot see every 12x slip, so state the unit on every line.

magnitudes.quantity: safety factor of a bolt, weld or member
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: designs usually land between about 1.5 and 4. The generous bounds only catch values that cannot be a real design check.
magnitudes.note: Below 1 may be the true answer to a 'will it hold' question, so check it rather than dismiss it. Above about 20: the load or the area is off by a unit factor (lbf vs kip, in^2 vs mm^2).

magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: fillet welds on plate and bracket work run from about 1/8 in to 1 in legs.
magnitudes.note: About 0.7x the expected leg: the throat was reported as the leg (leg = throat / 0.707). Far larger than the plate thickness: the weld group's unit moment of inertia or J is off by a units factor.

magnitudes.quantity: relative change in a time-stepped result when the step is halved
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: an explicit first-order scheme's error shrinks roughly in proportion to the step, so a step small enough to trust changes the result by only a few percent when halved. Numerical-methods property.
magnitudes.note: Tens of percent: the step is too large for the dynamics, or the update uses the current value instead of the previous one. Zero change: the step is not actually being used in the update.
